**Top 5 Brazilian universities in the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2025**

| Rank (global band) | University (Portuguese / English) | 2025 THE World University Ranking |
|---|---|---|
| **1st** | **Universidade de São Paulo (USP)** – Brazil | **201–250** (top of Brazil’s list)【7†L1-L9】 |

*These bands come from the “World University Rankings 2025” announcement and the USP news article that lists Brazil’s five highest‑ranked institutions by global band.*

---

### Placements of these universities in **2022** (THE World University Rankings)

| Year | Position (overall) | Country | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **2022** | **#2 (Latin America)** – *University of São Paulo* | Brazil | Held second place in the Latin America section of the THE rankings【8†L1-L4】 |

| **2022** | **151–175 (Overall)** – *State University of Campinas* (Unicamp) | Brazil | Same band as above for overall world ranking【10†L1-L4】 |
| **2022** | **601–800 (Overall)** – *UFRJ* & *UFRGS* | Brazil | Both fall in the 601–800 band for the 2022 overall ranking【7†L1-L4】 |

**Summary**

- In **2025**, USP leads Brazil, followed by Unicamp, Unesp, UFRJ and UFRGS.  
- In **2022**, USP was the top Brazilian university in Latin America (#2), Unicamp was third (#3); both were also ranked inside the 81–90 range for reputation and in the 601–800 band for overall world standing.

- Times Higher Education press release announcing the 2025 World University Rankings (includes Brazil’s presence and USP’s 201–250 slot).

## World University Rankings 2025

You are viewing a past edition of our rankings.

Explore the *Times Higher Education* World University Rankings 2025 below. Trusted worldwide by students, teachers, governments and industry experts, the list ranks 2,092 institutions from 115 countries and territories.

## University rankings 2025: highlights

- Oxford holds on to the top spot for the ninth consecutive year, bolstered by significant improvements in industry engagement and teaching
- MIT rises to second place, overtaking Stanford, which drops to sixth
- China edges closer to the top 10, further boosting its global research influence
- Australia’s top five universities all slip down the rankings, due to declining reputation and international outlook
- Three new countries join the top 200 - Brazil, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates - highlighting the rise of emerging markets in higher education

# Study in Brazil

Perhaps best-known for its sport and breathtaking scenery, Brazil is home to more than 2,500 universities, with elite institutions including the University of São Paulo, the biggest public university in the country and one of the best in Latin America. Also home to São Paulo State University, Brazil’s largest city and financial capital is also considered the nation’s cultural centre, home to a plethora of museums, art galleries and concert halls - and it has a vibrant nightlife.

Brazil’s 8,000km of coastline include thousands of spectacular beaches. Also unmissable is carnival season, which starts in February. Rio de Janeiro’s carnival is the biggest in the world, with more than two million people lining the streets each day to witness more than 300 bands and samba schools.

Brazil produces a third of the world’s coffee and is renowned for a wide variety of street food. The country's football team has won the World Cup more than any other nation, and football, by far the most popular sport, has been likened to a religion in the country. But many also like volleyball and, to a slightly lesser extent, mixed martial arts and basketball. Famous Brazilians include footballer Pelé and the late Formula 1 racing driver Ayrton Senna.

Public universities have free tuition for home and international students, but places are limited and most students attend private institutions.

### Brazilian government evaluation

Higher education evaluations are also conducted by the Brazilian Government; specifically by **Inep** (Instituto Nacional de Estudos e
Pesquisas Educacionais; English: National Institute of Studies and Research). The Government uses a **General Index of Courses** (Portuguese: [Índice Geral de Cursos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Índice_Geral_de_Cursos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Índice Geral de Cursos (page does not exist)") [[pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Índice%20Geral%20de%20Cursos "pt:Índice Geral de Cursos")]; **IGC**) to determine the quality of Brazilian's higher education (graduate and post-graduate courses) in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). [Universidade de São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidade_de_São_Paulo "Universidade de São Paulo"), one of the most prestigious universities in the country, has been participating in the **IGC** since 2013 as part of a technical cooperation with **Inep** that will last three years, during which time the results concerning the university's courses will not be disclosed. Only then will the university decide whether to fully participate in the government evaluation.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_Brazil#cite_note-RUF-1)

tool_trace.content:
# University of São Paulo | World University Rankings

The University of São Paulo is a large Brazilian public university, and is considered one of country's more prestigious educational institutions.

Founded in 1934, the University of São Paulo came about through a collaboration of existing schools such as the Faculdade de Direito do Largo de São Francisco (Law), the Polytechnic School (Engineering) and the Escola Superior de Agricultura Luiz de Queiroz (Agriculture).

Now, the university has created new departments, and is one of the largest institutions of higher education in Latin America.

Four of its eleven campuses can be found in the city of São Paulo while the remaining campuses are in the cities of Bauru, Lorena, Piracicaba, Pirassununga, Ribeirão Preto and two in São Carlos.

The university has an remarkable 70 libraries installed across the various campuses for students to use and enjoy.

A significant proportion of scientific papers published by Brazilian researchers are produced at the University of São Paulo.

The university also houses five affiliated hospitals, 24 museums and galleries – with half a million visitors per year – two theatres, a cinema, and its own TV channel run by students.

However, the University of São Paulo have no accommodation within campus, or outside. The search for accommodation must be carried out by students in accordance to their economic conditions and interests.

Notable alumni include Antonio Candido de Mello e Souza, a Brazilian writer, professor, sociologist and literary critic, Brazilian lawyer and Vice President Michel Miguel Elias Temer Lulia, and Guido Mantega, Brazil's former Finance Minister.

# Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2025 released

- Oxford overtakes California Institute of Technology and Harvard’s records in the number one spot as Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) has become the highest-ranked US university for the first time overtaking Stanford University.
- The reputation of UK and US universities have both significantly declined this year.
- The number of countries in the top 200 increased by three to 30 this year. They are: Brazil, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates.
- Seven countries are ranked for the first time: Bahrain, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Mongolia, Paraguay, Rwanda, Syria and Uzbekistan.
- The 21st year of the ranking has a record 2,092 universities ranked – up from 1,907 last year – from 115 countries and regions.
- The US has the most institutions ranked with 174, followed by Japan with 119, and joint third are UK and India with 107 each.

**Oxford University enjoys record-breaking year at the top, but US and UK sectors face drops in reputation**

The University of Oxford takes the top spot for a record-breaking ninth consecutive year in the*Times Higher Education* (*THE*) World University Rankings 2025, released today. Oxford has beaten Harvard University’s previous record of eight consecutive years at the number one spot from 2004 to 2011.

However, the reputation of the UK higher education sector is increasingly fragile as its top universities have declined for the second year in a row as the sector faces a severe financial crisis. The UK recorded the worst year-on-year decline in research reputation among large countries (with at least 50 ranked institutions). UK universities received 19 per cent of votes (for teaching and research combined) in the survey in 2016, compared with 15 per cent today.

US universities dominate the top 10 taking seven spots. Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) is now the highest-ranked US university in second place, its best-ever performance, while Stanford University dropped from second to sixth. The country has 23 universities in the top 50, 38 in the top 100 and 55 in the top 200 – more than any other country.

But the global reputation of US universities is at a record low. American universities received 47 per cent of the votes (for teaching and research combined) in *THE*’s 2016 reputation survey and this dropped sharply to 38 per cent this year - the steepest long-term decline of any country.

***THE*****’s top 10 universities in the world**

| **University** | **Country** | **Rank 2025** | **Rank 2024** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| University of Oxford | United Kingdom | 1 | 1 |
| Massachusetts Institute of Technology | United States | 2 | 3 |
| Harvard University | United States | 3 | 4 |
| Princeton University | United States | 4 | 6 |
| University of Cambridge | United Kingdom | 5 | 5 |
| Stanford University | United States | 6 | 2 |
| California Institute of Technology | United States | 7 | 7 |
| University of California, Berkeley | United States | 8 | 9 |
| Imperial College London | United Kingdom | 9 | 8 |
| Yale University | United States | 10 | 10 |

After two years of decreasing participation, the number of **Chinese mainland** universities surged back up to 94 this year and of those 26 improved on last year’s positions and six fell – a net change of +20; an improvement rate of 21 per cent. **Chinese mainland** had the second-highest improvement rate of all countries in the ranking, coming behind only **Sweden**, which saw seven universities improve and three drop down – an improvement rate of 31 per cent.

In 2021, the **US** had 59 universities in the top 200; this has now dropped to 55. The **UK**’s top 200 has also decreased since 2021, from 29 to 25, and Germany’s from 21 to 20. **Chinese mainland** and **Japan** are the only countries to increase their representation in the top 200 by more than one during this time, by six and three respectively. Chinese mainland now has 13 and Japan has five.

While the **UK**’s total has remained largely stable since 2021, the number of **Indian** institutions has risen rapidly in the past two years – jumping up to 107 in the 2025 edition from 75 in the 2023 edition. **Turkey** has also experienced fast growth, increasing from 43 in the 2021 edition to 91 in the 2025 edition.

Over the past five years, **Asia** has contributed the most new entrants to the ranking. Of the 211 universities that joined the ranking for the first time since the 2021 edition, 60 per cent are from **Asia**, 17 per cent from **Europe**, 10 per cent from **Africa**, and 10 per cent from **South America**.

**Egypt** saw the highest increase in the number of universities, adding seven new institutions since last year. **Nigeria** followed with an increase of six universities. In Europe, **France** experienced the largest growth with six additional universities. In South America, both **Brazil** and **Argentina** added five universities each.

Arab countries are doing exceptionally well with universities from **Saudi Arabia** and the **United Arab Emirates** entering the top 200. **Sub-Saharan Africa** has seen participation increase by 26 per cent year-on-year with ranked universities increasing from 42 last year to 53 this year. The highest-ranked university in **Africa** is University of Cape Town in joint 180th.

The **Latin America region** sees a university enter the top 200 this year with **Brazilian** institution University of São Paulo at joint 199th – its best performance for more than a decade. A record 166 universities from 13 countries are ranked from the region.

The 21st edition of the ranking has 2,092 universities ranked – up from 1,907 last year – from 115 countries and regions. This marks an increase of 9.7 per cent since last year, making it the biggest rise in the past five years and comparing to a 6 per cent growth last year.

The *THE* **World University Rankings 2025** are the most comprehensive, rigorous and balanced global ranking assessing research-intensive universities across 18 performance indicators, which are divided into five pillars, covering their core missions of teaching, research, knowledge transfer and internationalisation.

**Phil Baty, Times Higher Education’s chief global affairs officer, said**: “Oxford University’s achievement of being ranked first in the world for a record nine years, in a row, in *Times Higher Education*’s World University Rankings, is just an unbelievably phenomenal achievement.

“It is all the more impressive given the ever-increasing competition in our ranking as more and more universities participate each year with more than 2,000 assessed this year.

“I want to make a special point of congratulating every ranked university - simply being included in the ranking is something to celebrate as we focus on a couple of thousand global research universities among the tens of thousands of higher education institutions worldwide.

“*Times Higher Education’s* World University Rankings is the world’s gold-standard for ranking research-intensive universities. It’s unparalleled in participation, rigour and is the most trusted and respected ranking of its kind – where we have taken 21 years to carefully build up its reputation and prestige.”

This year 2,860 institutions submitted data, up six per cent on last year (last year it was 2,674) from 133 countries and territories. The World University Rankings 2025 has 2,092 ranked universities meaning 768 institutions gained “reporter” status, which means, although they submitted data, they did not meet *THE*’s eligibility criteria to receive a ranking.

The *THE* World University Rankings started with 200 universities and now has more than 2,000 making it the most global and inclusive ranking in the world.

***View the full [World University Rankings 2025 results](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2025/world-ranking) and see [World University Rankings 2025 methodology](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/world-university-rankings-2025-methodology).***

# USP is the highest-ranked Latin American university in the THE World Ranking – Jornal da USP

## USP is the highest-ranked Latin American university in the THE World Ranking

## In addition to USP, Unicamp and Pontifícia Universidade Católica of Chile are the best universities in Latin America

24/10/2025 - Publicado há 1 ano

## By: Erika Yamamoto

## Art by: Simone Gomes

![](https://jornal.usp.br/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/20251009_ranking-2026.jpg)

Photo:[Times Higher Education – THE](https://sinter.ufsc.br/2025/10/09/resultado-da-ufsc-no-world-university-rankings-2026-da-times-higher-education/)

[![](https://jornal.usp.br/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/read-portuguese.png)](https://jornal.usp.br/institucional/usp-e-a-latino-americana-mais-bem-classificada-no-the-world-ranking/)USP is the best Latin American university, according to the THE World University Rankings, one of the main international university rankings. Compiled by the British consultancy Times Higher Education (THE), the ranking was released on October 9.

Ranked in the 201-250 group, USP is on par with institutions such as the University of Illinois (United States), University of Surrey (United Kingdom), University of Wollongong (Australia), Tianjin University (China), and Tel Aviv University (Israel).

At the top of the list is the University of Oxford, followed by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT); Princeton University and the University of Cambridge are tied for third place. American institutions hold seven of the top ten positions.

USP improved in 9 of the 18 indicators adopted by the ranking: academic reputation, number of PhD graduates, budget, PhD/bachelor’s ratio, research reputation, research investments, number of international students, international collaboration, and industry funding acquisition.

“This year, a positive highlight in this ranking is the Teaching pillar, where we improved in four out of five indicators and rose from 78th to 68th place worldwide. In the Research Environment pillar, we stand at 107th globally, and in the Industry pillar, at 128th,” says Fátima Nunes, coordinator of USP’s Office for Management of Academic Performance Indicators (Egida).

![Fátima Nunes - Foto: Arquivo Pessoal](https://jornal.usp.br/wp-content/uploads/elementor/thumbs/20220628_fatima-pqzhlrs5qd8cci27dgr34llzirdfcb16us3v47wf9g.jpg "20220628_fatima")											Fátima L. S. Nunes - Photo: Courtesy of Fátima L. S. Nunes

In total, Brazil has 59 classified institutions. The State University of Campinas (Unicamp) is the second best-positioned Brazilian institution, in the group between 351-400. Following are the São Paulo State University (Unesp), the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), and the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), in the group of 601-800.

In this year’s edition, the ranking evaluated about 2,100 higher education institutions from 115 countries. The evaluation considered 18 indicators, grouped into five axes: Teaching, Research Environment, Research Quality, Industry, and Internationalization.

| --- | --- | --- |
| 1º | University of Oxford | United Kingdom |
| 2º | Massachusetts Institute of Technology | United States of America |
| =3º | Princeton University | United States of America |
| =3º | University of Cambridge | United Kingdom |
| =5º | Harvard University | United States of America |
| =5º | Stanford University | United States of America |
| 7º | California Institute of Technology | United States of America |
| 8º | Imperial College London | United Kingdom |
| 9º | University of California, Berkeley | United States of America |
| 10º | Yale University | United States of America |
| **201-250** | **Universidade de São Paulo (USP)** | **Brazil** |
| 351-400 | Universidade Estadual de Campinas (Unicamp) | Brazil |
| 401-500 | Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile (PUC-Chile) | Chile |

## International Recognition

USP also stood out in other international university rankings released this year. In the QS World University, prepared by Quacquarelli Symonds (QS), USP was the highest-ranked Brazilian university, in the 108th position. In the QS Latin America & The Caribbean Ranking, the University ranked second place.

In the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), prepared by the Chinese consultancy Shanghai Ranking Consultancy, USP was classified in the group between the 101st and 150th positions, being the highest-ranked Ibero-American university.

In another ranking by the Times Higher Education consultancy, the THE University Impact, USP ranked the 101-200th position. The ranking evaluates how universities worldwide are contributing to the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in terms of research, outreach, and governance.

More information on the ranking can be found on the page of USP’s [Office for Management of Academic Performance Indicators (Egida)](https://egida.usp.br/rankings/).

# USP é a latino-americana mais bem classificada no THE World Ranking 2025 - ABCD

[![](https://www.abcd.usp.br/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/USP-reconhecimento-internacional-240x300.jpg)](https://www.abcd.usp.br/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/USP-reconhecimento-internacional.jpg)A USP é a melhor universidade latino-americana, de acordo com o THE World University Rankings, um dos principais rankings universitários internacionais. Elaborado pela consultoria britânica Times Higher Education (THE), o ranking foi divulgado no dia 9 de outubro de 2025.

Esta é uma reprodução da matéria publicada no Jornal da USP [1].

Classificada no grupo de 201-250, a USP se iguala a instituições como a Universidade de Illinois (Estados Unidos), Universidade de Surrey (Reino Unido), Universidade de Wollongong (Austrália), Universidade Tianjin (China) e Universidade de Tel Aviv (Israel).

No topo da lista está a Universidade de Oxford, seguida pelo Instituto de Tecnologia de Massachusetts (MIT, na sigla em inglês); Universidade Princeton e Universidade de Cambridge estão empatadas na terceira colocação. Das dez primeiras posições, sete são de instituições norte-americanas.

A USP melhorou em 9 dos 18 indicadores adotados pelo ranking: reputação acadêmica, número de doutores titulados, orçamento, relação doutorados/bacharelados, reputação em pesquisa, investimentos em pesquisa, número de estudantes estrangeiros, colaboração internacional e captação de recursos da indústria.

*“Neste ano, o destaque positivo desse ranking fica para o eixo Ensino, em que melhoramos em 4 dos 5 indicadores e subimos da 78ª para a 68ª colocação global nessa dimensão. No eixo Ambiente de Pesquisa, estamos na 107ª posição global e no eixo Indústria, na 128ª colocação”*, destaca a coordenadora do Escritório de Gestão de Indicadores de Desempenho Acadêmico (Egida), Fátima Nunes.

Ao todo, o Brasil tem 59 instituições classificadas. A Universidade Estadual de Campinas (Unicamp) é a segunda brasileira mais bem posicionada, no grupo entre 351-400.

Em seguida, aparecem a Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp), a Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) e a Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), no grupo de 601-800.

Na edição deste ano, o ranking avaliou cerca de 2.100 instituições de ensino superior de 115 países.

A avaliação levou em conta 18 indicadores, agrupados em cinco eixos: Ensino, Ambiente de Pesquisa, Qualidade da Pesquisa, Indústria e Internacionalização.

**== Referência ==**

[1] YAMAMOTO, Érica. USP é a latino-americana mais bem classificada no THE World Ranking. **Jornal da USP**, 09 out. 2025. Disponível em: <https://jornal.usp.br/institucional/usp-e-a-latino-americana-mais-bem-classificada-no-the-world-ranking/>

The *Times Higher Education* World University Rankings 2022 include more than 1,600 universities across 99 countries and territories, making them the largest and most diverse university rankings to date.

# *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*

Annual publication of university rankings

**Times Higher Education World University Rankings**

| [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/74/WUR_logo_large.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WUR_logo_large.jpg) | |
| --- | --- |
| Editor | Phil Baty |
| Categories | [Higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") |
| Frequency | Annual |
| Publisher | *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* |
| First issue | 2004; 22 years ago (2004) (in partnership with *[QS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds")*)   2010; 16 years ago (2010) (on its own) |
| Country | [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") |
| Language | [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") & [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") |
| Website | [www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/) |

The ***Times Higher Education World University Rankings***, often referred to as the **THE Rankings**, is the annual publication of [university rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_ranking "University ranking") by the *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* magazine. The publisher had collaborated with [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds") (QS) to publish the joint *[THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* from 2004 to 2009 before it turned to [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") for a new ranking system from 2010 to 2013. In 2014, the magazine signed an agreement with [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier") to provide it with the data used in compiling its annual rankings.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-1)

The publication includes global rankings of universities, including by subject and reputation. It also has begun publishing three regional tables for universities in [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"), [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), and [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS") and emerging economies, which are ranked with separate criteria and weightings.

The THE Rankings is often considered one of the most widely observed university rankings together with the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")* and the *[QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings "QS World University Rankings")*.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4) It is praised for having a new, improved ranking methodology since 2010, but criticism and concerns have been voiced that this methodology underestimates [non-science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-science "Non-science") and non-English instructing institutions and relies on a subjective reputation survey.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-6)

## History

The creation of the original *[Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* has been attributed to [John O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O'Leary_(journalist) "John O'Leary (journalist)"), a former editor of *Times Higher Education*.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-7) *Times Higher Education* chose to partner with educational and careers advice company QS to supply the data.

After the 2009 rankings, *Times Higher Education* took the decision to break from QS and signed an agreement with Thomson Reuters to provide the data for its annual World University Rankings from 2010 onwards. The publication developed a new rankings methodology in consultation with its readers, its editorial board and Thomson Reuters. Thomson Reuters will collect and analyse the data used to produce the rankings on behalf of Times Higher Education. The first ranking was published in September 2010.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-8)

Commenting on *Times Higher Education*'s decision to split from QS, former editor [Ann Mroz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Mroz "Ann Mroz") said, "universities deserve a rigorous, robust and transparent set of rankings – a serious tool for the sector, not just an annual curiosity." She went on to explain the reason behind the decision to continue to produce rankings without QS' involvement, saying that: "The responsibility weighs heavy on our shoulders...we feel we have a duty to improve how we compile them."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-9)

Phil Baty, editor of the new *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, admitted in *[Inside Higher Ed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inside_Higher_Ed "Inside Higher Ed")*, "The rankings of the world's top universities that my magazine has been publishing for the past six years, and which have attracted enormous global attention, are not good enough. In fact, the surveys of reputation, which made up 40 percent of scores and which Times Higher Education until recently defended, had serious weaknesses. And it's clear that our research measures favored the sciences over the humanities."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-10)

He went on to describe previous attempts at peer review as "embarrassing" in *[The Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian "The Australian")*: "The sample was simply too small, and the weighting too high, to be taken seriously."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-11) THE published its first rankings using its new methodology on 16 September 2010, a month earlier than previous years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-timeshighereducation1-12)

In 2010, *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, along with the QS World University Rankings and the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")*, were described to be the three most influential international university rankings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-edmont-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-15) *[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Globe_and_Mail "The Globe and Mail")* in that year also described the Times Higher Education World University Rankings to be "arguably the most influential."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-16)

In 2014 *Times Higher Education* announced a series of important changes to its flagship THE World University Rankings and its suite of global university performance analyses, following a strategic review by THE parent company TES Global.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

## Methodology

### Criteria and weighting

The inaugural 2010–2011 [methodology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodology "Methodology") contained 13 separate indicators grouped under five categories: Teaching (30 per cent of final score), research (30 per cent), citations (research impact) (worth 32.5 per cent), international mix (5 per cent), industry income (2.5 per cent). The number of indicators is up from the Times-QS rankings published between 2004 and 2009, which used six indicators.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

A draft of the inaugural methodology was released on 3 June 2010. The draft stated that 13 indicators would first be used and that this could rise to 16 in future rankings, and laid out the categories of indicators as "research indicators" (55 per cent), "institutional indicators" (25 per cent), "economic activity/innovation" (10 per cent), and "international diversity" (10 per cent).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-19) The names of the categories and the weighting of each was modified in the final methodology, released on 16 September 2010[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The final methodology also included the weighting assigned to each of the 13 indicators, shown below[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) (with some updates from 2022 to 2023 released methodology[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-20)):

| Overall indicator | Individual indicator | Percentage weighting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Industry Income – innovation | Research income from industry (per academic staff) | 2.5% |
| International diversity (currently: International outlook (staff, students, research)) | Ratio of international to domestic staffRatio of international to domestic studentsInternational Collaboration (as for 2022–23) | 3% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2.5% (as for 2022–23) |
| Teaching – the learning environment | Reputational survey (teaching)PhDs awards per academicUndergrad. admitted per academicIncome per academicPhDs/undergraduate degrees awarded | 15%6%4.5%2.25%2.25% |
| Research – volume, income and reputation | Reputational survey (research)Research income (scaled)Papers per research and academic staffPublic research income/ total research income (currently cancelled) | 19.5% (18% as for 2022–23)5.25% (6% as for 2022–23)4.5% (6% as for 2022–23)/(currently cancelled, previously weighted 0.75%) |
| Citations – research influence | Citation impact (normalised average citation per paper) | 32.5% (30% as for 2022–23) |

The *Times Higher Education* billed the methodology as "robust, transparent and sophisticated", stating that the final methodology was selected after considering 10 months of "detailed consultation with leading experts in global higher education", 250 pages of feedback from "50 senior figures across every continent" and 300 postings on its website.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The overall ranking score was calculated by making [Z-scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") all datasets to standardize different data types on a common scale to better make comparisons among data.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The reputational component of the rankings (34.5 per cent of the overall score – 15 per cent for teaching and 19.5 per cent for research) came from an Academic Reputation Survey conducted by [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") in spring 2010. The survey gathered 13,388 responses among scholars who, according to THE, were "statistically representative of global higher education's geographical and subject mix."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) However, the response rate of the survey in 2022-2024 was a mere 1.8%.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-22) The magazine's category for "industry income – innovation" came from a sole indicator, institution's research income from industry scaled against the number of academic staff." The magazine stated that it used this data as "proxy for high-quality knowledge transfer" and planned to add more indicators for the category in future years.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

Data for [citation impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_impact "Citation impact") (measured as a normalized average citation per paper), comprising 32.5 per cent of the overall score, came from 12,000 [academic journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal") [indexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_index "Citation index") by Thomson Reuters' [Web of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_of_Science "Web of Science") database over the five years from 2004 to 2008. The *Times* stated that articles published in 2009–2010 have not yet completely accumulated in the database.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The normalization of the data differed from the previous rankings system and is intended to "reflect variations in citation volume between different subject areas," so that institutions with high levels of research activity in the [life sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_science "Life science") and other areas with high citation counts will not have an unfair advantage over institutions with high levels of research activity in the [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), which tend to use fewer citations on average.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The magazine announced on 5 September 2011 that its 2011–2012 World University Rankings would be published on 6 October 2011.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23) At the same time, the magazine revealed changes to the ranking formula that will be introduced with the new rankings. The methodology will continue to use 13 indicators across five broad categories and will keep its "fundamental foundations," but with some changes. Teaching and research will each remain 30 per cent of the overall score, and industry income will remain at 2.5 per cent. However, a new "international outlook – staff, students and research" will be introduced and will make up 7.5 per cent of the final score. This category will include the proportion of international staff and students at each institution (included in the 2011–2012 ranking under the category of "international diversity"), but will also add the proportion of research papers published by each institution that are co-authored with at least one international partner. One 2011–2012 indicator, the institution's public research income, will be dropped.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23)

On 13 September 2011, the *Times Higher Education* announced that its 2011–2012 list will only rank the top 200 institutions. Phil Baty wrote that this was in the "interests of fairness," because "the lower down the tables you go, the more the data bunch up and the less meaningful the differentials between institutions become." However, Baty wrote that the rankings would include 200 institutions that fall immediately outside the official top 200 according to its data and methodology, but this "best of the rest" list from 201 to 400 would be unranked and listed alphabetically. Baty wrote that the magazine intentionally only ranks around 1 per cent of the world's universities in a recognition that "not every university should aspire to be one of the global research elite."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-24) However, the 2015/16 edition of the Times Higher Education World University Rankings ranks 800 universities, while Phil Baty announced that the 2016/17 edition, to be released on 21 September 2016, will rank "980 universities from 79 countries".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-26)

The methodology of the rankings was changed during the 2011–12 rankings process, with details of the changed methodology here.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-27) Phil Baty, the rankings editor, has said that the THE World University Rankings are the only global university rankings to examine a university's teaching environment, as others focus purely on research.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-28) Baty has also written that the THE World University Rankings are the only rankings to put arts and humanities and social sciences research on an equal footing to the sciences.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-29) However, this claim is no longer true. In 2015, QS introduced faculty area normalization to their QS World University Rankings, ensuring that citations data was weighted in a way that prevented universities specializing in the Life Sciences and Engineering from receiving undue advantage.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-30)

In November 2014, the magazine announced further reforms to the methodology after a review by parent company TES Global. The major change being all institutional data collection would be bought in house severing the connection with [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"). In addition, research publication data would now be sourced from [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier")'s [Scopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopus "Scopus") database.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

### Reception

The reception to the methodology was varied.

Ross Williams of the [Melbourne Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Institute "Melbourne Institute"), commenting on the 2010–2011 draft, stated that the proposed methodology would favour more focused "science-based institutions with relatively few undergraduates" at the expense of institutions with more comprehensive programmes and undergraduates, but also stated that the indicators were "academically robust" overall and that the use of scaled measures would reward productivity rather than overall influence.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5) [Steve Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Smith_(academic) "Steve Smith (academic)"), president of [Universities UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_UK "Universities UK"), praised the new methodology as being "less heavily weighted towards subjective assessments of reputation and uses more robust citation measures," which "bolsters confidence in the evaluation method."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise2-31) [David Willetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Willetts "David Willetts"), British [Minister of State for Universities and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Business,_Innovation_and_Skills "Department for Business, Innovation and Skills") praised the rankings, noting that "reputation counts for less this time, and the weight accorded to quality in teaching and learning is greater."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise3-32) In 2014, David Willetts became chair of the TES Global Advisory Board, responsible for providing strategic advice to Times Higher Education.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-33)

### Criticism

Times Higher Education places a high importance on citations to generate rankings. Citations as a metric for effective education is problematic in many ways, placing universities who do not use English as their primary language at a disadvantage.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-34) Because English has been adopted as the international language for most academic societies and journals, citations and publications in a language different from English are harder to come across.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-35) Thus, such a methodology is criticized for being inappropriate and not comprehensive enough.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-RankingWatch-36) A second important disadvantage for universities of non-English tradition is that within the disciplines of social sciences and humanities the main tool for publications are books which are not or only rarely covered by digital citations records.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-37) In addition to these criticisms, the indicators used in the rankings have come under scrutiny. Several scholars, for example, have highlighted biases against [universities in the Arab region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_the_Arab_world "Higher education in the Arab world") within existing rankings. They have advocated for the development of new methodologies that account for institutional disparities and ensure fair representation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-39)

[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education") has also been criticized for its strong bias towards institutions that taught 'hard science' and had high quality output of research in these fields, often to the disadvantage of institutions focused on other subjects like the social sciences and humanities. For instance in the former [THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THE-QS_World_University_Rankings "THE-QS World University Rankings"), the [London School of Economics (LSE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London_School_of_Economics_and_Political_Science "The London School of Economics and Political Science") was ranked 11th in the world in 2004 and 2005, but dropped to 66th and 67th in the 2008 and 2009 edition.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-40) In January 2010, THE concluded the method employed by [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds"), who conducted the survey on their behalf, was flawed in such a way that bias was introduced against certain institutions, including LSE.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41)

A representative of [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"), THE's new partner, commented on the controversy: "*LSE stood at only 67th in the last Times Higher Education-QS World University Rankings – some mistake surely? Yes, and quite a big one*."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41) Nonetheless, after the change of data provider to Thomson Reuters the following year, LSE fell to 86th place, with the ranking described by a representative of Thomson Reuters as 'a fair reflection of their status as a world class university'.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-lse.ac.uk-42) [LSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") despite being ranked continuously near the top in its national rankings, has been placed below other British universities in the Times Higher Education World Rankings in recent years, other institutions such as [Sciences Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciences_Po "Sciences Po") have suffered due to the inherent methodology bias still used.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] [Trinity College Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College_Dublin "Trinity College Dublin")'s ranking in 2015 and 2016 was lowered by a basic mistake in data it had submitted; education administrator [Bahram Bekhradnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahram_Bekhradnia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bahram Bekhradnia (page does not exist)") said the fact this went unnoticed evinced a "very limited checking of data" "on the part of those who carry out such rankings". Bekhradnia also opined "while Trinity College was a respected university which could be relied upon to provide honest data, unfortunately that was not the case with all universities worldwide."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-43)

In general it is not clear who the rankings are made for. Many students, especially the undergraduate students, are not interested in the scientific work of a facility of higher education. Also the price of the education has no effects on the ranking. That means that private universities on the North American continent are compared to the European universities. Many European countries like France, Sweden or Germany for example have a long tradition on offering free education within facilities of higher education.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-45)

In 2021, the [University of Tsukuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tsukuba "University of Tsukuba") in [Ibaraki Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibaraki_Prefecture "Ibaraki Prefecture"), Japan, was alleged to have submitted falsified data on the number of international students enrolled at the university to the Times Higher Education World University Rankings.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) The discovery resulted in an investigation by THE and the provision of guidance to the university on the submission of data,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) however, it also led to the criticism amongst faculty members of the ease with which THE's ranking system could be abused. The matter was discussed in Japan's National Diet on April 21, 2021.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-47)

Seven Indian Institutes of Technology (Mumbai, Delhi, Kanpur, Guwahati, Madras, Roorkee and Kharagpur) have boycotted THE rankings from 2020. These IITs have not participated in the rankings citing concerns over transparency.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-48) [Sorbonne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbonne_University "Sorbonne University")'s President [Nathalie Drach-Temam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathalie_Drach-Temam "Nathalie Drach-Temam") announced in October 2025 that they would no longer participate in the Times Higher Education rankings. [Zurich University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich_University "Zurich University") had already made a similar move. Drach-Temam criticised the rankings because the methodologies were not transparent and they could not be reproduced or questioned. She called them "black boxes" and noted they were run by commercial companies.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-norank-49)

### Young universities

Additionally, *Times Higher Education* provides a ***THE Universities Under 50*** list (formerly only *150 Under 50 Universities*) with different weightings of indicators to accredit the growth of higher education institutions that are under 50 years old.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-63) In particular, the ranking attaches less weight to reputation indicators: for instance, the [University of Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Canberra "University of Canberra"), established in 1990, is placed at the 17th position, while the [Paris Sciences et Lettres University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Sciences_et_Lettres_University "Paris Sciences et Lettres University") (2010) is ranked 1st in 2023.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-64)

## World Reputation Rankings

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Reputation_of_Universities.png/250px-Reputation_of_Universities.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Reputation_of_Universities.png)Regions with universities included in the reputation league tables

*THE*'s ***World Reputation Rankings*** serve as a subsidiary of the overall league tables and rank universities independently in accordance with their scores in prestige.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-66)

Scott Jaschik of [Inside Higher Ed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inside_Higher_Ed "Inside Higher Ed") said of the new rankings: "...Most outfits that do rankings get criticised for the relative weight given to reputation as opposed to objective measures. While Times Higher Education does overall rankings that combine various factors, it is today releasing rankings that can't be criticised for being unclear about the impact of reputation – as they are strictly of reputation."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-67)

### Emerging economies

The *Times Higher Education* ***Emerging Economies Rankings*** (Formerly known as BRICS & Emerging Economies Rankings) only includes universities in countries classified as "emerging economies" by [FTSE Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTSE_Group "FTSE Group"), including the "[BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS")" nations of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. The **University of São Paulo** ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): *Universidade de São Paulo*, **USP**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university") [research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in the [Brazilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_of_Brazil "States of Brazil") of [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo_(state) "São Paulo (state)"), and the largest public university in Brazil.

The university was founded on 25 January 1934, regrouping already existing schools in the state of São Paulo, such as the [Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_School,_University_of_São_Paulo "Law School, University of São Paulo"), the [Polytechnic School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytechnic_School_of_the_University_of_São_Paulo "Polytechnic School of the University of São Paulo"), and the [College of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Agriculture,_University_of_São_Paulo "College of Agriculture, University of São Paulo"). The university's foundation in that year was marked by the creation of the [Faculty of Philosophy, Sciences and Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Philosophy,_Languages_and_Human_Sciences,_University_of_São_Paulo "Faculty of Philosophy, Languages and Human Sciences, University of São Paulo"), and subsequently new departments. Currently, the university is involved in teaching, research, and university extension in all areas of knowledge, offering a broad range of courses. It has eleven campuses, four of them in the [city of São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo "São Paulo").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-5) The remaining campuses are in the cities of [Bauru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bauru "Bauru"), [Lorena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorena,_São_Paulo "Lorena, São Paulo"), [Piracicaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracicaba "Piracicaba"), [Pirassununga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirassununga "Pirassununga"), [Ribeirão Preto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeirão_Preto "Ribeirão Preto") and two in [São Carlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Carlos "São Carlos").

University of São Paulo alumni and faculty include past or present 13 [Brazilian presidents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_Brazil "List of presidents of Brazil"), members of the [National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Congress_of_Brazil "National Congress of Brazil"), and founders and executives of notable Brazilian companies. Regarding research, USP is among Brazil's largest research institutions, producing more than 25% of the scientific papers published by Brazilian researchers in high-quality conferences and journals.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-6)

## History

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Henrique_Manzo_-_Retrato_de_Jos%C3%A9_Feliciano_Fernandes_Pinheiro_%28Visconde_de_S%C3%A3o_Leopoldo%29%2C_Acervo_do_Museu_Paulista_da_USP.jpg/250px-Henrique_Manzo_-_Retrato_de_Jos%C3%A9_Feliciano_Fernandes_Pinheiro_%28Visconde_de_S%C3%A3o_Leopoldo%29%2C_Acervo_do_Museu_Paulista_da_USP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Henrique_Manzo_-_Retrato_de_José_Feliciano_Fernandes_Pinheiro_(Visconde_de_São_Leopoldo),_Acervo_do_Museu_Paulista_da_USP.jpg)

The Viscount of São Leopoldo, precursor of the [São Paulo Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_School,_University_of_São_Paulo "Law School, University of São Paulo"), the oldest body of the University of São Paulo, in 1827

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/92/Pintura_Oficial_de_Armando_de_Sales.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pintura_Oficial_de_Armando_de_Sales.jpg)

[Armando de Sales Oliveira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armando_de_Sales_Oliveira "Armando de Sales Oliveira"), intervenor of São Paulo and of the University of São Paulo, in 1934

After its defeat in the [Constitutionalist Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutionalist_Revolution "Constitutionalist Revolution"), [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo "São Paulo") needed institutional improvements. Therefore, in 1933, a group of businessmen founded the *Free School of Sociology and Politics* (ELSP) (the current Foundation of the *School of Sociology and Politics* in São Paulo). In 1934, the intervenor of São Paulo (which corresponded to the governor), Armando de Sales Oliveira, founded the University of São Paulo (USP).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-7)

That was one of the efforts to provide Brazil with modern administrative, educational, and military institutions in a period known as "the search for alternatives." One of the main initiatives included the founding, that same year, of the University of São Paulo. Its nucleus was the School of Philosophy, Sciences, and Languages, with professors from France, Italy, Spain, Germany, and other European countries. The ELSP (Escola Livre de Sociologia e Política) assumed the goal of administrative elites to form a new model in which they noted an increasing role of the state. At the same time, USP (Universidade de São Paulo) focused on training teachers for secondary schools, experts in sciences, engineers, lawyers, physicians, and professors. The ELSP followed a sociological American model, while USP used the French academic world as its primary source of inspiration.

Foreign professors such as [Claude Lévi-Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lévi-Strauss "Claude Lévi-Strauss") (France), [Fernand Braudel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernand_Braudel "Fernand Braudel") (France), [Roger Bastide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Bastide "Roger Bastide") (France), Robert H. Aubreton (France), [Heinrich Rheinboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Rheinboldt "Heinrich Rheinboldt") (Germany), Paul Arbousse Bastide (France), Jean Magüé (France), [Martial Gueroult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_Gueroult "Martial Gueroult") (France), [Emilio Willems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Willems "Emilio Willems") (Germany), [Donald Pierson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Pierson "Donald Pierson") (US), [Gleb Vassielievich Wataghin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleb_Wataghin "Gleb Wataghin") ([Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia")), [Pierre Monbeig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Monbeig "Pierre Monbeig") (France), [Giacomo Albanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Albanese "Giacomo Albanese") ([Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")), [Luigi Fantappiè](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Fantappiè "Luigi Fantappiè") (Italy), [Vilém Flusser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilém_Flusser "Vilém Flusser") (Czech Republic), [Giuseppe Ungaretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Ungaretti "Giuseppe Ungaretti") (Italy) and [Herbert Baldus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Baldus "Herbert Baldus") (Germany), broadcast in various institutions new standards for teaching and research, creating new generations of scientists in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil").

Since its foundation USP received professors and researchers from all over the world, such as [David Bohm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bohm "David Bohm") (US), [Giuseppe Occhialini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Occhialini "Giuseppe Occhialini") (Italy), [François Châtelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/François_Châtelet "François Châtelet") (France), [Anatol Rosenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatol_Rosenfeld "Anatol Rosenfeld") (Germany), Helmi Nasr (Egypt), Gérard Lebrun (France), [Fritz Köberle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Köberle "Fritz Köberle") ([Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria")), [Alexander Grothendieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grothendieck "Alexander Grothendieck") (France), and Heinz Dieter Heidemann (Germany).

### Origins

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Faculdade_medicina_usp.jpg/250px-Faculdade_medicina_usp.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Faculdade_medicina_usp.jpg)

The [Faculty of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Medicine "Faculty of Medicine") in the early twentieth century.

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Faculdade_de_Direito_de_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Faculdade_de_Direito_de_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Faculdade_de_Direito_de_São_Paulo_(cropped).jpg)

The [Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_School "Law School") in 1880 during [Pedro II's reign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_II_of_Brazil "Pedro II of Brazil")

The University of São Paulo is the result of a combination of the newly founded School of Philosophy, Sciences and Languages (Faculdade de Filosofia, Ciências e Letras, FFCL, currently the [Faculty of Philosophy, Languages and Human Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Philosophy,_Languages_and_Human_Sciences,_University_of_São_Paulo "Faculty of Philosophy, Languages and Human Sciences, University of São Paulo") – Faculdade de Filosofia, Letras e Ciências Humana*s*, FFLCH)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-8) with the existing [Polytechnic School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytechnic_School_of_the_University_of_São_Paulo "Polytechnic School of the University of São Paulo") of Engineering (founded in 1893), the Luiz de Queiroz College of Agriculture ([Escola Superior de Agricultura Luiz de Queiroz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escola_Superior_de_Agricultura_Luiz_de_Queiroz "Escola Superior de Agricultura Luiz de Queiroz")) (founded in 1901), the Medical School (founded in 1912), the traditional [Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculdade_de_Direito_da_Universidade_de_São_Paulo "Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de São Paulo") (founded in 1827), the old School of Pharmacy and Dentistry (founded in 1898), the Institute of Astronomy, Geophysics and Atmospheric Sciences (founded in 1886), and the School of Veterinary Medicine (founded in 1919).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-www5.usp.br-9)

The FFCL emerged as the integrating element of the university, bringing together courses in various areas of knowledge. Also, in 1934, the *School of Physical Education* (sports science) of the State of São Paulo was created, the first civil school of physical education in Brazil, which would later be part of the university. In 1944, the Medical School opened its public hospital (*[Hospital das Clínicas da Universidade de São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_das_Clínicas_da_Universidade_de_São_Paulo "Hospital das Clínicas da Universidade de São Paulo")*). The School of Engineering of Sao Carlos (EESC) emerged in the same year. In subsequent years, several other research units were also created, such as a second Medical School located in the city of [Ribeirão Preto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeirão_Preto "Ribeirão Preto") (São Paulo's inland) in 1952.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-www5.usp.br-9)

In the 1960s, the university gradually transferred the headquarters of some of its units to the *City University Armando de Salles Oliveira*, in São Paulo. In 1963, the [Heart Institute of the University of São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_Institute_of_the_University_of_São_Paulo "Heart Institute of the University of São Paulo") was founded. After that, new institutes and schools were created, for instance, the *[School of Journalism, Communications and Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escola_de_Comunicações_e_Artes "Escola de Comunicações e Artes")* (ECA) in 1966. Over the years, some of the university's old departments were transformed into autonomous faculties or institutes, such as the *Institute of Biomedical Sciences* (ICB), the *Institute of Geosciences* (IGc), and the *Institute of Biosciences* (IB) in 1969.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-www5.usp.br-9)

### Military dictatorship

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Foto_antiga_do_Centro_Universit%C3%A1rio_Maria_Ant%C3%B4nia_da_Universidade_de_S%C3%A3o_Paulo.jpg/250px-Foto_antiga_do_Centro_Universit%C3%A1rio_Maria_Ant%C3%B4nia_da_Universidade_de_S%C3%A3o_Paulo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Foto_antiga_do_Centro_Universitário_Maria_Antônia_da_Universidade_de_São_Paulo.jpg)Students protesting against the [military government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_dictatorship_in_Brazil "Military dictatorship in Brazil") in front of one of the university's buildings.

During the 1970s and part of the 1980s, some critics believed that USP underwent an intellectual dissection in terms of knowledge production and the quality of human resources. During the past decades, the university played an essential role in the discussion and dissemination of important political ideas that contributed to the democratization of the country, bringing together many leftist intellectuals (such as [Florestan Fernandes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florestan_Fernandes "Florestan Fernandes"), Boris Fausto, Paul Singer, [Antonio Candido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Candido "Antonio Candido"), [Gioconda Mussolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gioconda_Mussolini "Gioconda Mussolini") among others).

During the [Brazilian dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_military_regime "Brazilian military regime"), a large number of professors from USP were persecuted and even tortured – many were forced to leave the country.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-12) This slowed down scientific production in Brazil.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-13) It also promoted a systematic increase in the total number of graduate vacancies, encouraged by the state government.

The gap caused by the removal of teachers and students chased by the [military regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_regime "Military regime") was interrupted by the campaign of political amnesty in the early 1980s. Several units of USP celebrated the return of their deposed professors, although many of them were rehired under different conditions (former [full professors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_professor "Full professor") took new positions as assistant professors).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-14)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Biblioteca_FAU-USP_1.jpg/250px-Biblioteca_FAU-USP_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Biblioteca_FAU-USP_1.jpg)The most recent [Architecture and Urbanism College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_and_Urbanism_College,_University_of_São_Paulo "Architecture and Urbanism College, University of São Paulo")'s building

### Expansion

Parallel to the resulting intellectual emptiness of political repression in the 1960s-80s, academic units were fragmented; new faculties and institutes were created, resulting in new courses, new lines of research, and [graduate programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduate_program "Graduate program"). Originally conceived as the university's academic core – gathering itself the various fields of knowledge – the FFCL (*School of Philosophy, Sciences and Letters*) saw its departments gain autonomy and become separate units. The *[Institute of Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Physics_of_the_University_of_São_Paulo "Institute of Physics of the University of São Paulo")* was the first department to extricate itself from the old FFCL, followed by other natural science departments.

In 2004, the university founded the *[Institute of International Relations](http://www.iri.usp.br/)* to study global matters in a multidisciplinary environment (law, political science, economy, and history) with Brazilian and international students and professors (*International Exchange Program*).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-15) In 2005, it was built in the East Zone of the [city of São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_São_Paulo "City of São Paulo") a new *[School of Arts, Sciences, and Humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Arts,_Sciences,_and_Humanities_at_the_University_of_São_Paulo "School of Arts, Sciences, and Humanities at the University of São Paulo")* (EACH), taking a few courses that go beyond the traditional Brazilian university model and aim to diversify the areas of the consolidated institution. [22] On 21 March 2006, USP approved the merger of a second *School of Chemical Engineering* (FAENQUIL) in the city of Lorena (rural area), at the [Paraíba Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraíba_Valley "Paraíba Valley") ([State of São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_São_Paulo "State of São Paulo")'s rural area), with about 1,600 students in total and of these 1,200 at graduation. In 2007, a second Law School was established in the city of [Ribeirão Preto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeirão_Preto "Ribeirão Preto"), also in the [State of São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_São_Paulo "State of São Paulo")'s countryside.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-16)

## Academics

Today, USP has five hospitals and offers 247 undergraduate programs and 239 graduate programs in all areas of study.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-International_Office-17) The university houses altogether 24 museums and galleries – with half a million visitors a year – two theaters, a cinema, a TV channel and an orchestra.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-International_Office-17) The University of São Paulo welcomes people from all continents and stimulates this process via networks and consortiums ([International Office – USP](http://www.usp.br/internationaloffice/en/)), such as [Erasmus Mundus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus_Mundus "Erasmus Mundus"), Associação das Universidades de Língua Portuguesa, and Rede Magalhães (SMILE – Student Mobility in Latin America, Caribbean and Europe), among others.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-18)

### Library system

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Biblioteca_florestan_fernandes_frontal.jpg/250px-Biblioteca_florestan_fernandes_frontal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Biblioteca_florestan_fernandes_frontal.jpg)The Florestan Fernandes Library at the [Faculty of Philosophy, Languages and Human Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Philosophy,_Languages_and_Human_Sciences,_University_of_São_Paulo "Faculty of Philosophy, Languages and Human Sciences, University of São Paulo").

USP has 42 libraries managed by the Integrated Library System (*SIB – Sistema Integrado de Bibliotecas* in Portuguese), which is also responsible for the university's online system, DEDALUS.

Dedalus is an online database that allows simultaneous consultation in all university libraries. It is also integrated into a system named Integrated Research, which integrates all online databases signed by the university. This makes academic research faster and provides researchers with easy access to international publications.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

- Teaching Assistant (Auxiliar de Ensino)—MS-2 (must have a master's degree and be enrolled in a doctoral program). Undergraduate students can also be teaching assistants for a semester, with scholarships from each department.

- Full Professor (Professor Titular) – MS-6 (top rank, only MS-6 professors can hold positions such as the Dean of a Faculty/School or the university's Rector).

## Admissions

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Fachada_do_Pr%C3%A9dio_da_Fuvest.jpg/250px-Fachada_do_Pr%C3%A9dio_da_Fuvest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fachada_do_Prédio_da_Fuvest.jpg)The [FUVEST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FUVEST "FUVEST") building, where the main admission exams are managed.

Brazilian students take USP's entrance exam, the [vestibular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestibular "Vestibular"), which is prepared and administered by [FUVEST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FUVEST "FUVEST") (University Foundation for Vestibular), subject to regulations approved by the university's Undergraduate Studies Council. In 2012, 159,603 students signed up for Fuvest's vestibular for 10,982 openings. Candidates must take a multiple-choice test involving chemistry, physics, mathematics, biology, geography, history, Portuguese, and English. The second round of tests is written and specific to the chosen field of studies, including more in-depth questions in physics, chemistry, and mathematics for engineering; history, math, and geography for law; and so on. In-depth written Portuguese questions are required for all.

More recently, students have also been able to access the university by taking the nationwide high school evaluation test, ENEM, through the [Unified Selection System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_de_Seleção_Unificada "Sistema de Seleção Unificada") (SISU). Each undergraduate course manages the vacancies available for each admission process.

International students may come through several exchange programs. In 2012, USP hosted over 2,300 exchange students. Roughly a third of the international students are enrolled in humanities and social sciences, with another third in engineering courses.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo#cite_note-34)

USP does not require its students, national or foreign, to pay any tuition, as its source of funding comes from the state of São Paulo.

## Organization

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/University_of_Sao_Paulo_campus_2016_008.jpg/250px-University_of_Sao_Paulo_campus_2016_008.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Sao_Paulo_campus_2016_008.jpg)Seat of the USP Rectory.

USP corresponds to the idea of "university" as a set of autonomous schools, institutes, and colleges, each responsible for one area of knowledge (the aforementioned thirty-six teaching, research, and extension). Like most Brazilian universities, it grants autonomy to its teaching, research, and extension units regarding the didactic organization and curricular definition of each of the courses, which often results in a considered excessive fragmentation of teaching and research and the disconnection between the knowledge produced in each of the units.

Each unit is divided into departments. A department is usually responsible for one of the courses offered by the unit or for a specific search line. In the case of units with only one or two courses, departments are not responsible for the entire course but for a part of it. Due to the aforementioned fragmentation and decentralization of the university, it is common to see departments with similar profiles in different units, which raises criticism as to the effectiveness of public investments and duplication of efforts.

### Administration

The administrative structure of USP has in the [Rectory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectory "Rectory") its central organ, as well as in the [Rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recto "Recto") the main figure of the university. Subordinated to the Rectory are the four Pro-Rectorates, specialized agencies in each of the university's fields of activity: *Pro-Rectorate* (PRG), *Post-Graduation Pro-Rectorate* (PRPG), *Pro-Rectory of Research* (PRP) and *Pro-Rectory of Culture and Extension* (PRC).

In recent years, there has been discussion about creating a *Pro-Rectorate for Student Assistance,* a subject that, according to critics, has always been considered secondary to the university's leaders.
